g.text: Windowed and temporal joins — two operations, not two settings
windowed: 5 matches, up to 5 buffered, 2 click never emits · temporal: 5 enriched at once, 2 NULL
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · "a" = clicks, "b" = impressions · join window 60s
every candidate pair, and whether it matches
5 of the 20 candidate pairs are within 60s. The window bounds the buffer; the watermarks bound the wait.
Note one click matches 2 impressions — a windowed join is not one-to-one, so the output can be larger than either input.
Step 1/4 — the windowed join: match within a time interval
The join predicate is one subtraction, and it produces 5 matches from 20 candidates. Worth noticing in the note: one click matches 2 impressions,
so a windowed join can emit more rows than either side has — which is a capacity question people usually discover after shipping.
Windowed and temporal joins — two operations, not two settings
windowed: 5 matches, up to 5 buffered, 2 click never emits · temporal: 5 enriched at once, 2 NULL
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · "a" = clicks, "b" = impressions · join window 60s
TEMPORAL (STREAM-TABLE) JOIN — the version current at click time
one lookup per row, against the table as it stood at that event time
NULL — no impression exists at or before 12:00:01
NULL — no impression exists at or before 12:00:03
No window, no buffer, no wait — each row is enriched from the table immediately. 2 rows gets NULL because the table had no version yet at that
What it DOES need is a VERSIONED table: the lookup is "as of 12:02:10", not "now".
Step 2/4 — the temporal join: look up the table AS OF the row's time
A temporal join is a lookup, and it behaves completely differently: all 5 clicks are enriched immediately, with no buffer and no wait. The price
is in the note — it needs the table's **history**, because "as of 12:02:10" is not the same question as "now", and a table that only holds current
Windowed and temporal joins — two operations, not two settings
windowed: 5 matches, up to 5 buffered, 2 click never emits · temporal: 5 enriched at once, 2 NULL
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · "a" = clicks, "b" = impressions · join window 60s
SIDE BY SIDE, ON THE SAME DATA
not two implementations of one idea — two different operations
windowed: the 60s window · temporal: the table, finite per key
windowed: up to 5 rows · temporal: nothing
windowed: when both watermarks pass · temporal: immediately
windowed: watermarks on both sides · temporal: a VERSIONED table
The windowed join waits because a match may still arrive. The temporal join does not, because the table's version at that event time is already
That is why 2 clicks never emits under the windowed join and all 5 emit under the temporal one.
Step 3/4 — so the two joins are bounded by entirely different things
The row that matters is the third. A windowed join waits because a counterpart may still arrive; a temporal join does not, because the table's
state at that event time is already settled. On this data that is the difference between 2 click never emitting and all 5 emitting at once.
Windowed and temporal joins — two operations, not two settings
windowed: 5 matches, up to 5 buffered, 2 click never emits · temporal: 5 enriched at once, 2 NULL
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · "a" = clicks, "b" = impressions · join window 60s
the diagnosis is about the INPUT, not about the join configuration
results arrive late, or not at all, for no apparent reason
a windowed join against what is really a slowly-changing table
2 of 5 rows never emit, and 2 true matches are withheld
read the right-hand input: dimension-like → temporal join
Widening the window or lengthening allowed lateness treats the symptom and makes the state worse — the wait was never needed.
The question to ask is "could this side still produce a row that changes an old answer?" If not, it is a table.
Step 4/4 — and mistaking one for the other is the common bug
The reason this bug survives is that the obvious fixes look reasonable: widen the window, raise allowed lateness. Both grow the state and neither
helps, because the wait was never necessary. The diagnostic question is whether the right-hand side can still produce a row that changes an old
answer — and for a dimension table it cannot.
